## Biological rationale

CD45RA is not an independent gene product — it is an epitope carried by specific **isoforms of PTPRC (CD45)**. PTPRC pre-mRNA undergoes alternative splicing of three extracellular "variable" exons (exon 4/A, 5/B, 6/C). Anti-CD45RA antibodies (e.g., HI100) recognize an exon-4(A)-dependent epitope, whereas the shortest isoform, which skips all three variable exons, carries the CD45RO epitope and is invisible to anti-CD45RA. Because PTPRC is transcribed by essentially every nucleated leukocyte, **total PTPRC mRNA is a poor predictor of CD45RA surface signal**; two cells with identical PTPRC transcript abundance can differ enormously in CD45RA staining purely on the basis of exon 4 inclusion versus skipping.

Exon 4 choice is cell-state dependent and mechanistically characterized: naive, antigen-inexperienced lymphocytes include exon 4 (CD45RA-high), while memory/activated T cells and monocytes skip it (CD45RO-dominant, CD45RA-low) — the classic naive→memory CD45RA→CD45RO switch (Akbar et al., 1988; Hermiston et al., 2003). The switch is executed by RNA-binding repressors — **PTBP1/PTB, hnRNP L, and SFPQ/PSF** — acting through exonic splicing silencers in exon 4 (Lynch & Weiss, 2000; Rothrock et al., 2005; Topp et al., 2008). SFPQ is itself under signaling control: GSK3-mediated phosphorylation targets SFPQ for degradation in resting cells (permitting exon 4 inclusion → CD45RA), while activation-driven PI3K–Akt inhibition of GSK3 stabilizes SFPQ and drives exon skipping (→ CD45RO) (Heyd & Lynch, 2010). A single disease-associated polymorphism in exon 4 (C77G) is sufficient to perturb this splicing and alter CD45 isoform display (Motta-Mena et al., 2010), confirming that exon 4 handling directly controls CD45RA antibody reactivity.

This matters especially in **cord blood**: neonatal CBMCs are overwhelmingly antigen-inexperienced — naive T cells (TCF7/LEF1/CCR7/SELL-high recent thymic emigrants), transitional/naive B cells (which express full-length CD45RABC and stain CD45RA+), and immature NK cells — all predicted CD45RA-high — alongside CD14+ monocytes and rare in-utero-activated/memory-phenotype lymphocytes, predicted CD45RA-low. (Nucleated erythroid precursors, common in cord blood, lack PTPRC entirely and form the trivial CD45-negative floor.)

## Committed hypothesis

**Cell-to-cell variation in surface CD45RA across CBMCs is governed by the cell-state-dependent alternative splicing of PTPRC exon 4 (the "A" exon): naive/resting lymphoid cells (naive T, B, NK) include exon 4 and display high CD45RA, whereas monocytes and activated/memory-programmed lymphocytes repress exon 4 inclusion via the PTBP1–hnRNP L–SFPQ silencer axis (stabilized when PI3K–Akt signaling inhibits GSK3), producing CD45RO isoforms and low CD45RA despite comparable total PTPRC mRNA.**

## Falsifiable experimental tests

1. **In-data test:** CD45RA antibody-derived tags should correlate weakly with total PTPRC RNA but strongly with lineage/state — high on TCF7+/LEF1+/SELL+ naive T cells, MS4A1+/CD79A+ B cells, and KLRD1+ NK cells; low on CD14+/LST1+/S100A8+ monocytes and any activated (HLA-DRA-high) or memory-skewed lymphocytes.
2. **Isoform test:** Exon-junction-aware analysis (reads spanning the exon 3–4 junction = inclusion vs. exon 3–7 junction = skipping; or targeted long-read/single-cell full-length sequencing, or RT-PCR across exons 3–7 on flow-sorted CD45RA-hi vs. CD45RA-lo cells) should show that exon 4 inclusion — not total PTPRC — predicts the CD45RA ADT rank order of cells.
3. **Perturbation test:** Sort CD45RA+ cord blood naive T cells and stimulate ex vivo (anti-CD3/CD28). Exon 4 skipping and the CD45RA→CD45RO surface switch should emerge within ~48–96 h *without* loss of total PTPRC mRNA. The switch should be accelerated by GSK3 inhibition (CHIR99021) or SFPQ/PTBP1 overexpression, and blunted by PTBP1/hnRNP-L/SFPQ knockdown or by maintaining GSK3 activity via PI3K–Akt inhibition. Loss of surface CD45RA with preserved total PTPRC transcript would confirm the splicing mechanism over a transcriptional one.

## Established vs. new

This is primarily **(a) established literature knowledge**: the exon-4 dependence of the CD45RA epitope, the naive→memory CD45RA→CD45RO splicing switch, and the PTBP1/hnRNP-L/SFPQ–GSK3 regulatory axis are well documented (Akbar et al., 1988; Hermiston et al., 2003; Lynch & Weiss, 2000; Heyd & Lynch, 2010; Motta-Mena et al., 2010), and CD45RA is a standard antibody in CBMC CITE-seq panels (Stoeckius et al., 2017). The **(b) new, testable component** is its single-cell instantiation: that exon-junction-resolved PTPRC isoform usage — not total PTPRC — explains the RNA–protein discordance for CD45RA in neonatal CBMCs, and that manipulating the GSK3–SFPQ axis shifts surface CD45RA in primary human neonatal cells, which has not to my knowledge been directly demonstrated at single-cell resolution.
